claim: Pupils tend to dilate in response to surprising events.
source: Pupils tend to dilate in response to surprising events, but it is not known whether these responses are primarily stimulus driven or instead reflect a more nuanced relationship between pupil-linked arousal systems and cognitive expectations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that references established knowledge in the field.

claim: Evoked pupil diameter is more parsimoniously described as signaling violations of learned, top-down expectations than changes in low-level stimulus properties.
source: Using an auditory adaptive decision-making task, we show that evoked pupil diameter is more parsimoniously described as signaling violations of learned, top-down expectations than changes in low-level stimulus properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both baseline and evoked pupil diameter is modulated by the degree to which individual subjects use violations to update their subsequent expectations.
source: We further show that both baseline and evoked pupil diameter is modulated by the degree to which individual subjects use these violations to update their subsequent expectations, as reflected in the complexity of their updating strategy.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pupil size changes primarily as a function of ambient light levels.
source: Pupil size changes primarily as a function of ambient light levels but also in the context of a host of other brain functions that often involve changes in arousal (Joshi and Gold, 2020; Mathôt, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pupil size is modulated by brain functions that involve changes in arousal.
source: Pupil size changes primarily as a function of ambient light levels but also in the context of a host of other brain functions that often involve changes in arousal (Joshi and Gold, 2020; Mathôt, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Early studies ascribed arousal-related modulations of pupil size to 'mental effort' required for tasks like solving arithmetic problems or holding items in working memory.
source: Several early studies ascribed arousal-related modulations of pupil size to the 'mental effort' required to, for example, solve an arithmetic problem or hold items in working memory (Beatty, 1982; Mathôt, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mental effort view of pupil modulations emphasizes the idiosyncratic and cognitive nature of pupil fluctuations but lacks a precise description of the computations being encoded.
source: This view emphasizes the idiosyncratic and cognitive nature of these pupil fluctuations but lacks a precise description of the computations being encoded.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior literature presented in the introduction.

claim: Pupil size is sensitive to stimulus probabilities, typically increasing when unexpected stimuli are presented or expected stimuli are omitted.
source: Pupil size is also sensitive to stimulus probabilities, typically increasing when unexpected stimuli are presented or expected stimuli are omitted (Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Qiyang et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Arousal-related pupil modulations represent critical computations required to learn from and adapt to changes in the environment.
source: More recently, arousal-related pupil modulations have been shown to represent critical computations required to learn from, and adapt to, changes in our environment (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Nassar et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Preuschoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rapid phasic increases in pupil size occur in response to surprising events that can drive changes in beliefs.
source: Rapid phasic increases in pupil size occur in response to surprising events that can drive changes in beliefs (Nassar et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Preuschoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slower tonic increases in pupil size can encode increased belief uncertainty.
source: Slower tonic increases in pupil size can encode increased belief uncertainty (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Muller et al., 2019; Nassar et al., 2012; Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slower pupil changes are most closely linked with changes in mental effort.
source: These slower pupil changes are also those most closely linked with changes in mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Mathôt, 2018) and associated with individual differences in cognitive traits such as fluid intelligence (Tsukahara et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slower pupil changes are associated with individual differences in cognitive traits such as fluid intelligence.
source: These slower pupil changes are also those most closely linked with changes in mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Mathôt, 2018) and associated with individual differences in cognitive traits such as fluid intelligence (Tsukahara et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptive decision-making has been studied primarily in relatively stable environments where changes to stimulus properties occur infrequently.
source: First, adaptive decision-making has been studied primarily in relatively stable environments, in which changes to stimulus properties occur infrequently and are therefore almost always 'surprising' (Filipowicz et al., 2016; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Nassar et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous stable environment studies conflate violations of top-down cognitive expectations with bottom-up sensory responses to stimulus changes.
source: These environments thus conflate violations of top-down, cognitive expectations that govern surprise with more basic bottom-up sensory responses to stimulus changes that can also modulate pupil size (e.g., 'startle' or 'orienting' responses; Bremner, 2009; Sara, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior literature with supporting citations.

claim: Seventy-eight subjects performed an auditory predictive-inference task.
source: Seventy-eight subjects performed an auditory predictive-inference task that required them to predict on each trial which of two source locations (left or right) would generate an auditory tone (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The source generating the tones switched locations at unannounced points throughout the task.
source: The source generating the tones switched locations from right-to-left or left-to-right at unannounced points throughout the task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The per-trial probability of source-location switch (hazard rate) was fixed at either a low (H = 0.01), intermediate (H = 0.30), or high (H = 0.99) value in blocks of trials.
source: The per-trial probability of this source-location switch, or 'hazard rate' (H), was fixed at either a low (H = 0.01), intermediate (H = 0.30), or high (H = 0.99) value in blocks of trials that changed at unannounced points throughout the task (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Uncertainty was added by playing the tone from the opposite side of the generating source on 20% of trials.
source: To make this inference process more challenging, uncertainty was added by playing the tone from the opposite side of the generating source on 20% of trials ('opposite-location trials').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Subjects adjusted their behavior adaptively to different hazard rates on average.
source: On average, the subjects adjusted their behavior adaptively to different hazard rates.
evidence: This is a summary statement of behavioral results.

claim: The proportion of correct predictions was above chance for all hazard-rate conditions.
source: Across subjects, the proportion of correct predictions was above chance for all hazard-rate conditions, with the highest performance for low hazard rates (median [interquartile range, or IQR] proportion correct = 0.82 [0.79–0.85], 0.59 [0.56–0.61], and 0.63 [0.56–0.67] for low, intermediate, and high hazard rates, respectively; two-tailed signed-rank test for H0: median = 0.5, all ps < 4.2×10−12; two-tailed paired rank-sum test for H0: per-subject performance difference between hazard pairs = 0, all ps ≤ 0.0009).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data.

claim: Performance was highest for low hazard rates.
source: Across subjects, the proportion of correct predictions was above chance for all hazard-rate conditions, with the highest performance for low hazard rates (median [interquartile range, or IQR] proportion correct = 0.82 [0.79–0.85], 0.59 [0.56–0.61], and 0.63 [0.56–0.67] for low, intermediate, and high hazard rates, respectively; two-tailed signed-rank test for H0: median = 0.5, all ps < 4.2×10−12; two-tailed paired rank-sum test for H0: per-subject performance difference between hazard pairs = 0, all ps ≤ 0.0009).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data.

claim: In the low hazard-rate condition, source-location switches were relatively rare and unexpected.
source: Specifically, in the low hazard-rate condition, source-location switches from one side to the other were relatively rare and therefore unexpected.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental design and task structure.

claim: In the low hazard-rate condition, performance was low for trials on which the source location switched.
source: Accordingly, performance was low for trials on which the source location switched (because subjects reasonably assumed that the switch on that trial was from the 20% of opposite-location trials) but then gradually increased over several trials as the subject gathered more evidence that a real source-location switch had occurred.
evidence: This statement is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Hazard-dependent behavioral patterns were roughly consistent with simulated behavior from a Bayesian learning model.
source: These hazard-dependent behavioral patterns were roughly consistent with simulated behavior from a Bayesian learning model that used trial-by-trial observations to perform inference over both the current source and hazard rate (Figure 1c,d; Glaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of behavioral data to model simulations shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Subjects' pupils dilated in response to tone presentation.
source: In general, the subjects' pupils dilated in response to tone presentation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnitude of evoked pupil response was negatively correlated with the corresponding baseline pupil diameter.
source: The magnitude of this evoked pupil response was negatively correlated with the corresponding baseline pupil diameter (median [IQR] Spearman's rho comparing trial-by-trial baseline pupil diameter to baseline-subtracted evoked change per subject = −0.34 [−0.41 – −0.26], sign-rank test for H0: median = 0, p=1.1×10−10), as has been reported previously (de Gee et al., 2014; Gilzenrat et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of pupil data and citations to prior work.

claim: In the low and intermediate hazard-rate conditions, evoked changes in pupil diameter tended to be larger when the tone location switched than when it repeated.
source: Specifically, in the low and intermediate hazard-rate conditions, the evoked changes in pupil diameter tended to be larger when the tone location switched than when it repeated from the previous trial.
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the low hazard-rate condition, the effect of tone location switches on evoked pupil responses persisted into the next baseline.
source: This effect persisted into the next baseline for the low, but not the intermediate, hazard-rate condition (Figure 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the high hazard-rate condition, evoked pupil responses were not modulated systematically by whether or not the sound location switched.
source: Conversely, in the high hazard-rate condition, the evoked pupil responses were not modulated systematically by whether or not the sound location switched (Figure 2c), but baseline pupil diameter on the subsequent trial tended to be larger after the source location repeated than when it switched on the previous trial (Figure 2b).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the high hazard-rate condition, baseline pupil diameter on the subsequent trial tended to be larger after the source location repeated than when it switched.
source: Conversely, in the high hazard-rate condition, the evoked pupil responses were not modulated systematically by whether or not the sound location switched (Figure 2c), but baseline pupil diameter on the subsequent trial tended to be larger after the source location repeated than when it switched on the previous trial (Figure 2b).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the low and intermediate hazard-rate conditions, baseline pupil diameter was larger on trials in which the subject would predict a source location switch versus repeat.
source: Specifically, in the low and intermediate hazard-rate conditions, in which switches were unexpected, the baseline pupil diameter (measured prior to the subject hearing the tone and then making a prediction on that trial) was larger on trials in which the subject would then hear the tone and subsequently predict that the source location would switch versus repeat on the next trial (Figure 2b).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the low and intermediate hazard-rate conditions, evoked pupil responses were larger when the subject predicted a location switch versus repeat.
source: The subsequent evoked pupil response showed an additional modulation in the same direction, corresponding to larger evoked dilations when the subject predicted a location switch versus repeat (Figure 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the high hazard-rate condition, baseline and evoked changes in pupil diameter tended to be larger when predictions repeated from the previous trial.
source: In contrast, in the high hazard-rate condition, in which switches were expected, baseline and evoked changes in pupil diameter tended to be larger when predictions repeated from the previous trial (Figure 2a,c).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pupil responses to errors were modulated by the hazard rate, with pupils dilating more to errors on tone-switch trials in the low hazard-rate condition and to errors on tone-repeat trials in the high hazard-rate condition.
source: Additionally, these pupil responses to errors were modulated by the hazard rate, such that pupils tended to dilate more to errors on tone-switch trials in the low hazard-rate condition, and to errors on tone-repeat trials in the high hazard-rate condition (measured as the tone-switch by error interaction in all three hazard conditions; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by pupil data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pupil size was modulated by context-specific predictions and their violations.
source: Together these results show that pupil size was modulated by not just low-level stimulus properties (tone-location switches) but also context-specific predictions and their violations, corresponding to location switches when stability was expected and repetitions when instability was expected.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the pupil data presented in Figure 2.

claim: A Bayesian learning model was fit to each subject's trial-by-trial sequence of behavioral choices.
source: To better relate the task-dependent pupil modulations to the specific belief-updating strategies each individual subject used to derive hazard-specific predictions, we fit each subject's trial-by-trial sequence of behavioral choices (predictions) with a Bayesian learning model that performs inference over both the source location and hazard rate (Glaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the modeling approach.

claim: A key parameter in the Bayesian learning model controls the width of the distribution of prior probabilities that subjects assign to different hazard rates.
source: A key parameter in the model controls the width of the distribution of prior probabilities that subjects assign to different hazard rates, with wider prior distributions leading to model predictions that adapt more effectively to changes in hazard rate than narrower prior distributions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure with reference to a figure.

claim: Belief strength was quantified as the log-odds-ratio that source 1 versus 2 would generate the next tone.
source: Using the per-subject model fits, we quantified belief strength on each trial as the log-odds-ratio that source 1 versus 2 would generate the next tone (Gold and Shadlen, 2001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about how belief strength was computed, with a citation.

claim: Surprise was quantified as the negative log probability that the observed tone was predicted.
source: We quantified surprise on each trial as the negative log probability that the observed tone was predicted (Filipowicz et al., 2018; Mars et al., 2008; O'Reilly et al., 2013), which reflected the degree to which the new observation did not match the current belief about location (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about how surprise was computed, with citations.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter encoded belief strength from the belief-updating process.
source: Baseline and evoked pupil diameter encoded belief strength and surprise, respectively, from this belief-updating process (Figure 3a,b shows results from linear regressions of pupil diameter that accounted for relationships between baseline and evoked pupil diameter as in Figure 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows comparable results using a linear regression of the first temporal derivative of evoked changes in pupil diameter, which is thought to be less susceptible to baseline effects; de Gee and Tsetsos, 2019; Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Evoked pupil diameter encoded surprise from the belief-updating process.
source: Baseline and evoked pupil diameter encoded belief strength and surprise, respectively, from this belief-updating process (Figure 3a,b shows results from linear regressions of pupil diameter that accounted for relationships between baseline and evoked pupil diameter as in Figure 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows comparable results using a linear regression of the first temporal derivative of evoked changes in pupil diameter, which is thought to be less susceptible to baseline effects; de Gee and Tsetsos, 2019; Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Baseline pupil diameter was negatively correlated with belief strength, such that baseline pupil diameter was smaller when beliefs about the next source were more certain.
source: In particular, baseline pupil diameter was negatively correlated with the idiosyncratic model-derived belief strength (i.e., inverse uncertainty derived from subject-specific model fits), such that baseline pupil diameter was smaller when beliefs about the next source were more certain (Figure 3a).
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Evoked changes in pupil diameter were closely associated with surprise, with more surprising stimuli evoking larger pupil dilations.
source: After the tone was heard, evoked changes in pupil diameter were closely associated with surprise, with more surprising stimuli evoking larger pupil dilations with a time course similar to the switch modulations (Figure 3b).
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Pupils dilated slightly less after tone onset if beliefs were very strong, regardless of surprise.
source: Evoked change also reflected information about the prediction belief strength before having heard the tone, such that pupils dilated slightly less after tone onset if beliefs were very strong, regardless of surprise.
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Response times tended to be shorter on trials when beliefs were more certain.
source: Similar effects were evident in the subjects' behavioral response times (RTs), which tended to be shorter on trials when beliefs were more certain and longer on trials following the occurrence of a surprising stimulus (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Response times tended to be longer on trials following the occurrence of a surprising stimulus.
source: Similar effects were evident in the subjects' behavioral response times (RTs), which tended to be shorter on trials when beliefs were more certain and longer on trials following the occurrence of a surprising stimulus (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: There was a modest trial-to-trial correlation between RT after hearing the tone and changes in pupil diameter on the same trial.
source: These RT effects testify to the behavioral relevance of these model-derived quantities but did not alone account for their relationships with pupil size: although there was a modest trial-to-trial correlation between the RT after hearing the tone and changes in pupil diameter on the same trial (median [IQR] Spearman's rho computed per subject = 0.11 [0.06–0.18] for baseline pupil and 0.12 [0.07–0.18] for evoked pupil, sign-rank test for H0: median = 0, all ps < 3.7×10−7), baseline and evoked pupil changes showed the same strong modulations by belief strength and surprise, respectively, even when accounting for trial-by-trial RTs (Fig. Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of RT and pupil data.

claim: Baseline and evoked pupil changes showed strong modulations by belief strength and surprise even when accounting for trial-by-trial RTs.
source: These RT effects testify to the behavioral relevance of these model-derived quantities but did not alone account for their relationships with pupil size: although there was a modest trial-to-trial correlation between the RT after hearing the tone and changes in pupil diameter on the same trial (median [IQR] Spearman's rho computed per subject = 0.11 [0.06–0.18] for baseline pupil and 0.12 [0.07–0.18] for evoked pupil, sign-rank test for H0: median = 0, all ps < 3.7×10−7), baseline and evoked pupil changes showed the same strong modulations by belief strength and surprise, respectively, even when accounting for trial-by-trial RTs (Fig. Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A major component of individual variability on this task can be ascribed to differences in the complexity of each subject's belief-updating strategy.
source: We reported previously that a major component of individual variability on this kind of task can be ascribed to differences in the complexity of each subject's belief-updating strategy (Glaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Complexity measures the amount of past information a given belief-updating strategy encodes to predict future events.
source: Complexity measures the amount of past information a given belief-updating strategy encodes to predict future events, which captures the flexibility with which new observations are used to update the belief (Bialek et al., 2001; Gilad-Bachrach et al., 2003; Myung et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Complex strategies can be helpful if the past features they encode are useful for prediction but can also lead to errors if the past features they encode are irrelevant.
source: Complex strategies can be helpful if the past features they encode are useful for prediction (e.g., tracking today's temperature, barometric pressure, and weather trends to predict tomorrow's weather) but can also lead to errors if the past features they encode are irrelevant (e.g., using today's European weather trends to predict tomorrow's weather in New York).
evidence: This is an explanation of complexity with illustrative examples.

claim: A key signature of complexity is a trade-off between bias and variance.
source: Thus, a key signature of this form of complexity is a trade-off that is well known in statistics and machine learning between: 1) bias, or the (in) ability to flexibly update beliefs given new, relevant observations; and 2) variance, or the propensity to over-adjust beliefs given new, irrelevant (e.g., noisy) observations (Bishop, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Subjects who tended to adjust their beliefs appropriately to real changes in hazard rate also tended to have more variable choices even when the hazard rate remained fixed.
source: This bias-variance trade-off was evident in the present data set, such that subjects who tended to adjust their beliefs appropriately to real changes in hazard rate (low bias) also tended to have more variable choices even when the hazard rate remained fixed (high variance; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual differences in belief-updating complexity were characterized using an information-bottleneck analysis.
source: We characterized individual differences in belief-updating complexity using an information-bottleneck analysis (Palmer et al., 2015; Tishby et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method with citations.

claim: The information-bottleneck method provided a model-agnostic measure of the extent to which each subject's predictions relied on both stimulus and hazard-rate information.
source: This method provided a model-agnostic measure of the extent to which each subject's predictions relied on both stimulus and hazard-rate information, while also accounting for differences in the specific stimulus (tone-location) sequences that each subject experienced (Glaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method with a citation.

claim: Subjects using more complex strategies tended to have behavioral patterns that depended more strongly on the hazard-rate condition.
source: As expected given this definition of complexity, subjects using more complex strategies tended to have behavioral patterns that depended more strongly on the hazard-rate condition (Figure 4c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Individual differences in belief-updating complexity were reflected in task-driven pupil modulations.
source: These individual differences in belief-updating complexity were reflected in task-driven pupil modulations.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings presented in Figure 5.

claim: The relationship between baseline pupil fluctuations and complex belief strength became systematically stronger for subjects who were using increasingly complex belief-updating strategies.
source: This relationship between baseline pupil fluctuations and complex belief strength became systematically stronger (more negatively correlated) for subjects who were using increasingly complex belief-updating strategies (Figure 5).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A similar relationship with complexity was not evident in the surprise-modulated evoked-pupil responses.
source: A similar relationship with complexity was not evident in the surprise-modulated evoked-pupil responses (Figure 4b), possibly reflecting relatively stronger bottom-up modulation in evoked versus baseline pupil.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Subjects with more complex strategies tended to make predictions that better matched the objective hazard rate in each of the three hazard-rate conditions.
source: In general, subjects with more complex strategies tended to make predictions that better matched the objective hazard rate (assessed by fitting the normative choice model to behavior with subjective hazard rate as a free parameter in hazard-specific blocks; Glaze et al., 2015; Figure 6a) and have higher overall accuracy (Figure 6b) in each of the three hazard-rate conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Subjects with more complex strategies tended to have higher overall accuracy in each of the three hazard-rate conditions.
source: In general, subjects with more complex strategies tended to make predictions that better matched the objective hazard rate (assessed by fitting the normative choice model to behavior with subjective hazard rate as a free parameter in hazard-specific blocks; Glaze et al., 2015; Figure 6a) and have higher overall accuracy (Figure 6b) in each of the three hazard-rate conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both behavioral effects of complexity were most pronounced for the high hazard-rate condition.
source: Strikingly, however, both of these behavioral effects were most pronounced for the high hazard-rate condition.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Subjective hazard rates were most variable and most strongly mis-matched to objective values in the high hazard-rate condition.
source: First, subjective hazard rates were most variable and most strongly mis-matched to objective values (dotted lines in Figure 6a) in the high hazard-rate condition (F-test comparing the variance of fits for each hazard rate condition: low versus high, p=2.2×10−10; intermediate versus high, p=1.0×10−13; low versus intermediate, p=0.179).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical tests on data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Performance accuracy was furthest from the ceiling provided by a fully adaptive Bayesian learning model in the high hazard-rate condition.
source: Second, performance accuracy was furthest from the ceiling provided by a fully adaptive Bayesian learning model in the high hazard-rate condition (median [IQR] difference in accuracy compared with wide-prior model depicted in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a = 0.11 [0.08–0.15], 0.04 [0.03–0.07], and 0.29 [0.25–0.36] for the low, intermediate, and high hazard-rate conditions, respectively; two-tailed paired Wilcoxon tests comparing the difference in high versus low and intermediate hazards conditions, all ps < 8.5×10−10).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data.

claim: Response times were slowest in the high-hazard condition.
source: Third, RTs were slowest in the high-hazard condition (median [IQR] RT for all trials and subjects = 478 [381–560], 507 [415–635], and 641 [513–790] ms for the low, intermediate, and high hazard-rate conditions, respectively; two-tailed paired sign-rank test for H0: median difference = 0, all ps < 0.0007).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical tests on RT data.

claim: Subjects had more difficulty learning in the high hazard-rate condition despite the fact that the same level of accuracy could in principle be achieved in the high and low hazard-rate conditions.
source: Thus, despite the fact that the same level of accuracy could, in principle, be achieved in the high and low hazard-rate conditions, and that both conditions were more predictable than the intermediate hazard-rate condition, subjects had more difficulty learning in the high hazard-rate condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the behavioral data presented.

claim: Individual differences in belief-updating complexity were reflected in pupil diameter in the high, but not the low or intermediate, hazard-rate condition.
source: Consistent with these observations, individual differences in belief-updating complexity were reflected in pupil diameter in the high, but not the low or intermediate, hazard-rate condition.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: For subjects with complex strategies in the high hazard-rate condition, tone switches versus repeats tended to more strongly reinforce their belief, which corresponded to smaller baseline pupil diameter on the next trial.
source: Specifically, subjects with more complex belief-updating strategies were able to learn much more appropriate expectations and thus perform closer to ceiling than subjects with less complex strategies in the high hazard-rate condition. For these subjects with complex strategies, tone switches versus repeats tended to more strongly reinforce their belief (i.e., reduce their uncertainty) that the source had switched, which corresponded to smaller baseline pupil diameter on the next trial (Figure 7a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: For subjects with complex strategies in the high hazard-rate condition, subsequent tone switches versus repeats tended to be less surprising, which corresponded to smaller evoked pupil responses.
source: Based on these more appropriate expectations, subsequent tone switches versus repeats tended to be less surprising, which corresponded to smaller evoked pupil responses (Figure 7b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Task-driven modulations of pupil size reflected context-dependent violations of learned expectations and not just bottom-up stimulus changes.
source: First, task-driven modulations of pupil size reflected context-dependent violations of learned expectations and not just bottom-up stimulus changes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the first primary finding.

claim: Cognitively driven changes in both baseline and evoked changes in pupil size could be parsimoniously understood as representing belief strength and surprise, respectively.
source: Second, these cognitively driven changes in both baseline and evoked changes in pupil size could be parsimoniously understood as representing belief strength and surprise, respectively, associated with the subjects' trial-by-trial inferences about latent, task-relevant properties of the environment (in this case, a joint inference about the location of the source that would generate the next sound and the hazard rate that governed how often the location of the source switched from one side to the other).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the second primary finding.

claim: Pupil dynamics reflected not just average belief-updating processes but also how they were implemented by individual subjects.
source: Third, these pupil dynamics reflected not just average belief-updating processes but also how they were implemented by individual subjects, further testifying to their behavioral and cognitive relevance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the third primary finding.

claim: Cognitive modulations of pupil size do not simply reflect objective task difficulty.
source: According to our results, these modulations do not simply reflect: 1) objective task difficulty, because in our study objective difficulty was equivalent in the low and high hazard-rate conditions that had substantially different pupil responses; 2) overall performance, because performance was similar in the intermediate and high hazard-rate conditions that also had substantially different pupil responses; or 3) RTs, which were only weakly related to pupil diameter on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented.

claim: Tonic pupil-linked arousal is closely associated with a belief-updating process that aims to reduce uncertainty by interpreting new data according to multiple possible hypotheses.
source: Instead, our results suggest that tonic pupil-linked arousal is closely associated with a belief-updating process that aims to reduce uncertainty by interpreting new data according to multiple possible hypotheses (i.e., different hazard rates), which is consistent with a recent proposal that pupil-linked arousal encodes periods of information gain (Zénon, 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented, with a citation to related work.

claim: Pupil modulations are sensitive to the complexity of the belief-updating process, which may be related to traditional notions of cognitive load.
source: Our results extend this idea by showing that pupil modulations are also sensitive to the complexity of the belief-updating process, which may be related to traditional notions of cognitive load (Beatty, 1982; Mathôt, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented, with citations to related work.

claim: Subjects tended to adapt incompletely to relatively predictable environments, including over-estimating low hazard rates and under-estimating high hazard rates.
source: As we reported previously, subjects tended to adapt incompletely to relatively predictable environments, including over-estimating low hazard rates and under-estimating high hazard rates (Glaze et al., 2018; Glaze et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Incomplete adaptations were asymmetric between the low and high hazard-rate conditions, with considerably worse and more variable performance in the high hazard-rate condition.
source: Here we showed that, despite the fact that those two hazard-rate conditions were equally predictable, these incomplete adaptations were asymmetric between the two conditions, with considerably worse and more variable performance in the high hazard-rate condition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the low hazard-rate condition, belief updating could use congruent bottom-up and top-down information.
source: These asymmetric modulations of pupil and behavior reflected the fact that in the low hazard-rate condition, belief updating could use congruent bottom-up and top-down information (i.e., stimulus changes were surprising), whereas in the high hazard-rate condition, belief updating was based on top-down processing that was incongruent with bottom-up information (i.e., stimulus repeats were surprising).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented.

claim: In the high hazard-rate condition, belief updating was based on top-down processing that was incongruent with bottom-up information.
source: These asymmetric modulations of pupil and behavior reflected the fact that in the low hazard-rate condition, belief updating could use congruent bottom-up and top-down information (i.e., stimulus changes were surprising), whereas in the high hazard-rate condition, belief updating was based on top-down processing that was incongruent with bottom-up information (i.e., stimulus repeats were surprising).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented.

claim: Increases in pupil size have been tied to higher levels of activation of the brainstem nucleus locus coeruleus.
source: Increases in pupil size have been tied to higher levels of activation of the brainstem nucleus locus coeruleus (LC), which is the primary source of norepinephrine (NE) to the brain (de Gee et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2014; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptive gain theory proposes that tonic release of NE occurs during periods of active exploration.
source: Adaptive gain theory proposes that tonic release of NE occurs during periods of active exploration (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Aston-Jones et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There may be a form of 'mental exploration' that occurs when beliefs are weak and alternative explanations for the observed data are sought.
source: Specifically, although physical exploration is absent in our task, there may be a form of 'mental exploration' that occurs when beliefs are weak and alternative explanations for the observed data are sought in terms of the hypothesis space of possible hazard rates (e.g., the prior distribution over hazard rates in our Bayesian learning model; Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Glaze et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and prior work.

claim: Phasic, event-driven release of NE may result in widespread network 'resets' that interrupt and initiate the reorganization of neural networks engaged during a task.
source: Phasic, event-driven release of NE, possibly corresponding to evoked pupil changes in response to surprise as described in our and other studies (Joshi et al., 2016; Nassar et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Preuschoff et al., 2011), may play a complementary role in adaptive inference. Instead of promoting exploration, phasic NE release is thought to result in widespread network 'resets' that interrupt and initiate the reorganization of neural networks engaged during a task, possibly reducing previously learned biases and enhancing the relevance of new observations (Bouret and Sara, 2005; de Gee et al., 2017; Sara, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Network resets can occur for not just an abrupt, surprising change in sensory input, but also an abrupt, surprising lack of change in sensory input.
source: Our results suggest that this kind of network reset can occur for not just an abrupt, surprising change in sensory input, but also an abrupt, surprising lack of change in sensory input.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex is reciprocally connected with the LC and has been proposed to guide executive control.
source: One possible source of such information is the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), which is reciprocally connected with the LC and has been proposed to guide executive control, allocating when and how executive resources are used during cognitively demanding tasks (Filipowicz et al., 2016; Shenhav et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2016; Shenhav et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During adaptive decision-making, the ACC and the anterior insula are active when changes are detected and mental models are updated.
source: During adaptive decision-making, the ACC and the anterior insula are active when changes are detected and mental models are updated (Behrens et al., 2007; Donoso et al., 2014; McGuire et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019; Stöttinger et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.
